title: How to Run a Sample and Fit-Check Loop Before You List an Apliiq Product
excerpt: How to run a sample and fit-check loop before you list a product: which variables to isolate, what to record on a scorecard, and how to turn sample results into fewer sizing returns.
body: Most print-on-demand returns are not printing defects. They are expectation gaps: the blank fits differently than the photo suggested, the stitch density looks lighter in daylight, or the size chart was copied from a supplier who measures differently than you do. A sample loop closes those gaps before you spend money driving traffic to a listing that only generates tickets. Two rounds of samples cost less than one month of returns at scale.

Start by deciding what you are testing. Separate the product into three variables: the blank, the decoration method, and the size run. Order samples that isolate each one. Testing a new fleece blank? Order it in two sizes with the same embroidery. Testing placement? Keep the blank identical and move only the artwork. Changing more than one variable per round is the fastest way to receive a sample you cannot interpret.

Build a written scorecard before the box arrives. Record the measurements yourself: chest width, body length, sleeve length, and shoulder width, measured flat and kept in a spreadsheet with the product. Add decoration checks, such as whether small text stays legible at the chosen stitch density, whether a patch edge lifts after a wash, and whether a print cracks when stretched. Finish with one cold wash, one normal dry, and a re-measure.

Photograph the sample in the same lighting you will use for the product page, and hold the photo next to the supplier mockup. Every place where the two disagree is a place your returns come from. If the mockup renders a brighter shade than the physical garment, fix the mockup or describe the color accurately in the copy. Shoppers forgive a muted tone they were warned about. They do not forgive a shade that differs from the screen.

Wear the sample for a week before you list it. This is not a laboratory test, but it catches the failures that matter commercially: collars that curl after a few hours, prints that fade along the fold line, embroidery that snags on a bag strap. If it is not something you would wear, hand it to someone with a different body type. One honest opinion from a different fit beats a dozen approvals from people who all wear the same size.

Close the loop by writing the results into the listing. Replace the inherited size chart with your own measurements, add a fit note naming the model height and size worn, and flag any care requirement you found in testing. Then set a review date. Blank supplies change, and the hoodie that fit this season may come from a different mill next season. Re-order a sample whenever you change blanks or decoration partners.

If you are still shortlisting decoration partners while you build this loop, the DTCwise Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing. The Apliiq profile at /tool/apliiq covers the decoration methods and blank catalog it supports, which is the quickest way to confirm that a sample is worth paying for before you order one.
